name: Wunderdog Sports
title: Wunderdog Review 2026: Pricing, Record, Is It Worth It?
description: Wunderdog review, checked 20 Nov 2026: prices from $15 to $5,499, the free package guarantee, its own pick log checked, and what buyers say.
dek: A one man pick service run by a handicapper called Geoff, who sells as the Wunderdog and has posted picks since 2001. Packages run from $15 to $5,499 a year, and a losing package earns a free replacement package, never cash. The site keeps and grades its own public pick log; its long run totals show small profits at about 52% to 53% winners, while the free picks it gives away show a better record than the paid card as a whole.

status.label: Not verified
status.note: Watchdog has not graded a full, time stamped record for Wunderdog. Its pick archive is published and graded by Wunderdog itself. This page reports what we could check and labels everything else.

short_answer: Wunderdog is a real, long running business. It names a company, Wunderdog Sports Picks LLC, publishes every price, lists a phone line and email, and sells one person's picks. A 2008 university teaching case and a 2011 betting blog both refer to the service, so it has been around in some form for a long time. In that narrow sense it is legitimate.

It also does something most pick sellers do not: it posts an archive of past Pro Picks with the line, the price, the units, the result and the time each pick was released. The totals it shows are modest. The NFL line on 20 Nov 2026 was 3,264 wins and 2,905 losses for +196.76 units over 25.2 years, which works out to about 3 cents of profit per unit on each decided pick. That archive is kept and graded by Wunderdog itself, so we could not confirm it is complete.

Two details from its own numbers are worth knowing. The free picks it gives away show a much better record (NFL free picks 265-179, 59.7%) than the full paid card (52.9%), so judging the service by its free emails will flatter it. And the "Recent Performance" box on the about page shows a different slice for each sport, such as playoff picks only for the NBA and free picks only for the WNBA.

The guarantee replaces a losing package with another one free. It never returns cash, and the terms say there are no refunds once a product is delivered. Buyer talk is small and split: a few long time customers praise the honesty and the replacement packages, while a handful of one star reviews say they lost money and the guarantee only gave them more picks. If you buy, buy short, log every pick yourself with the price you actually got, and remember that even the seller's own long run numbers sit just above break even.

guarantee: The guarantee page says: "If my picks don't result in a profit for you (more units won than lost based on recommended unit plays) over the period of your package, with each sport in a combo calculated separately, you'll receive an equivalent package for free." Each package listing repeats it: "If this package does not show a profit (measured as positive net units won), you'll automatically receive an equivalent package free." Horse racing picks carry no guarantee, and the NFL office pool packages show no guarantee wording.

The support page calls this the Golden Guarantee and says the next set of picks is sent automatically. It also says that if Wunderdog passes on a day during a daily or weekly package, the package is extended by a day.

This is a replacement, not a refund. The terms page says "Once a product has been delivered, there are no refunds," and that on termination "no part of the Subscription Fee will be refunded." The guarantee is measured in Wunderdog's own units at its recommended sizes and posted prices, so a buyer who bets different amounts or gets worse lines can lose money while the package counts as a win. Two Trustpilot reviewers made exactly this complaint. Losses on the bets themselves are never covered, and those are usually far larger than the package price.

One more detail in the terms: they describe the subscription fee as a "capital contribution" to a Wunderdog Sports Trust, paid in exchange for access to digital services, with no equity or financial return. The terms do not explain why they are written this way. A buyer should simply understand that the terms promise picks, not money back.

claims_note: How we checked: Wunderdog prints its own running totals in boxes on its archive and past pick pages, in wins, losses and units. We read them on 20 Nov 2026 and did the arithmetic ourselves. Win rate is wins divided by wins plus losses; units per decided pick is the unit total divided by the same count. These are the seller's own figures; we did not regrade any pick apart from the spot check below.

Spot check: the past pick page for Miami at New York on 25 Oct 2026 says the pick was "released to clients on October 23, 2026 at 12:12PM ET" and shows "2 units on Miami +5 (-110)" with a final score of Miami 28, New York 25. Miami won outright, so the win is graded correctly.

The Harvard claim: we searched for a Harvard Business Review case study and did not find one. The case we found, "Wunderdog Sports Picks" (QA-0719), was published by the Darden School of Business on 8 Apr 2008 for an introductory statistics course. Its summary says it is an email from the owner of a picks service to a professor, claiming 87 of 149 correct NFL picks against the spread in 2005, and asks students to judge that claim. It is a lesson in evaluating a record, not an endorsement.

Numbers drift between pages. The homepage says 85,000+ documented picks and the about page 88,697. The all sports one year package is labeled "just $2 per pick" while its description says "about $1.00 per pick." The bettor count on the homepage banner fell from 401,222 to 400,210 in two weeks. None of this proves anything about the picks, but the marketing is not kept consistent.

To its credit, the long run totals Wunderdog advertises are modest and close to break even, not the 70% claims common in this business. Its about page says outright: "No one hits 80%, or 70% or even 60% long term."
record: What a buyer can verify independently: very little. We found no full, time stamped log kept by a third party, no contest results from an outside organizer that we opened, and no regulator or court record. The awards on the about page were not checked.

What Wunderdog itself publishes: sport archive pages list past Pro Picks back to 2001 for the NFL, by season and week, and each past pick page shows the write up, the units, the line, the price, the release time and a graded result. That is far more than most pick sellers show. But the archive is kept and graded by the seller, and we could not confirm that no pick is missing or changed.

What the seller's own numbers say: across its three biggest sports the paid card wins about 52% to 53% and makes roughly 0.02 to 0.03 units per decided pick. If those numbers are complete and accurate, they describe a small edge with long losing stretches, not a fast way to make money. A buyer who pays for picks and gets worse prices than the posted lines could easily end up behind.

Background: the support page says Wunderdog was born in 2001 when Geoff started posting picks on a friend's website. The about page says he studied statistics, earned a masters degree at a business school, worked in corporate and startup jobs, and began building an NFL model in the early 1990s. A September 2011 betting blog post described an ESPN interview with "Geoff Kulesa, founder of Wunderdog Sports Picks" and said he had worked in marketing at Hewlett Packard; we found no second source for the surname. The company is Wunderdog Sports Picks LLC, and its terms are governed by Colorado law. Today the picks are sold on wunderdog.com and, at $15 a week, through a Sports Illustrated Pro Picks storefront on Whop, and Wunderdog runs promotional blocks in VSiN's daily newsletter.

our_data.text: Watchdog grades picks captured from public posts before the game starts. In this edition Wunderdog is not matched to a Watchdog graded record, so we make no claim about how its picks perform beyond what the seller publishes.
our_data.context: For scale: Wunderdog's own NFL archive shows 52.9% winners over 25 years. On the Watchdog board, {{over60}} of {{established}} established accounts (100 or more graded picks) were at 60% or better, and the median established account won {{median_win}}% of its picks. At standard -110 odds a bettor needs about 52.4% to break even.

customers_intro: Independent customer evidence on Wunderdog is thin for a service this old. We found 10 Trustpilot reviews, a handful of short forum threads and posts on Sportsbook Review and TheRX, two Reddit posts, a store listing rating and seller chosen testimonials. Below is everything we found and how much weight it can carry.

customers.text: We found about 20 independent posts and reviews about Wunderdog from 2009 to 2026, on Trustpilot, Sportsbook Review, TheRX, Reddit, a store listing and a betting blog. The positive side is steady: long time customers on Trustpilot praise the write ups, the support staff and the free replacement package, a 2009 forum buyer said a season pass had won over 60%, and forum members in 2020 and 2024 called the service legitimate but a long term proposition. The negative side repeats one point: three one star Trustpilot reviews from 2025 and 2026 say they lost money and that the guarantee only gives more picks, not money back, and a fourth, from 2023, alleges the company scams customers, with no details. On TheRX and Reddit, members repost or hunt for its paid plays rather than discuss results. We found no buyer posting a full season result, no BBB profile and no court or regulator record.

Wunderdog runs a testimonials page and quotes customer notes on its homepage and guarantee page, including buyers who praise its honesty and the free replacement package. These are selected and published by the seller, so they cannot tell you what a typical buyer experiences.

Trustpilot showed a TrustScore of 3.6 from 10 reviews on a profile the company claimed in Nov 2025: six 5 star and four 1 star reviews, with company replies to two of the negative ones. Ten reviews is not a sample.
A reviewer who described himself as a long time customer praised the detailed analysis and said staff were helpful and quick to respond.

A reviewer reported heavy losses on a multi sport subscription, said a refund was refused and questioned the unit sizing. Wunderdog replied, disputed the size of the loss from the figures given and asked the reviewer to email for an account review.

A reviewer said a Game of the Month pick lost, the free replacement package started automatically, and he still finished down overall. He criticized the guarantee. Wunderdog's reply explained the automatic replacement, acknowledged he was down overall and offered a free package.
A reviewer said recent picks had done poorly and that the guarantee does not return the money spent.
A reviewer called the service trustworthy and said a technical glitch was fixed quickly, with a bonus pick offered.

A Trustpilot reviewer recommended the service and said its system wins about 60% of the time. That is well above the seller's own long run totals of about 53%, so it likely reflects the reviewer's own stretch.

Three five star Trustpilot reviews from 2024 praised a run of college football totals, the write ups and the free pick guarantee, and support that fixed a login problem. None gave a dollar or unit result.

A one star Trustpilot reviewer accused the company of scamming customers and mentioned an account that had been deleted. The review gives no amounts or details, and there is no company reply. This is one person's allegation, which we could not check.
On Sportsbook Review a member asked whether Wunderdog's NFL plays get posted on the forum and said a season pass bought the year before had been solid, winning over 60%. Nobody replied.

A Sportsbook Review member said three straight free Wunderdog picks had lost and asked whether that was a cold streak or a sign of a bad picker. The one substantive reply called the service legitimate, long running and a long term investment, and noted it gives out free plays, mostly football.

In a Sportsbook Review thread asking about handicapping services, a member said Wunderdog was the only service that came to mind, noted that its pick volume had grown compared with its first ten years, and suggested trying the free picks first to see whether they offer value.

On TheRX, where members repost paid plays, a Saturday service play thread listed a Wunderdog play on the Mets moneyline at -165. Members post the plays without grading them. Paid picks circulating for free is common for well known services.
A Reddit user in r/sportsbetting asked which service play forum was releasing Wunderdog's premium picks. It shows people hunting for the paid card for free, not a view on results.
A Reddit user comparing public betting percentages said the figures on Action Network, Wunderdog and Covers differed a lot. This is about Wunderdog's free consensus data, not its picks.

The Wunderdog listing on the Sports Illustrated Pro Picks storefront on Whop showed 4.8 out of 5 from 22 ratings, 18 five star and 4 four star. The review texts were not shown, so we cannot say what buyers liked.

A betting blog described an ESPN interview with the founder about week 1 NFL lines, praised the service's unemotional, numbers first approach and recommended it. The blog says it uses Wunderdog selections in its own systems, so it is a fan, not a neutral tester.

A Better Business Bureau search for Wunderdog returned no business profile. We found no Covers forum thread about the service, and two older Sportsbook Review threads about it required a login, so we did not read or use them.

conflicts: The support page says each Pro Pick includes "a link to the sportsbook where I found the best line." We could not see those links without buying, so we do not know whether they are affiliate links that pay Wunderdog. We saw no sportsbook promo codes or revenue share links on the public pages we opened.

Wunderdog advertises through VSiN: VSiN's partnership offers page lists a free $50 Wunderdog credit for VSiN subscribers, and VSiN's daily newsletter on 2 Nov and 15 Nov 2026 carried Wunderdog blocks offering a daily complimentary pick and a $50 credit, without a sponsored label on the block.
The terms say the site uses third party advertising companies to serve ads. We found no parent company or sportsbook ownership tie.
Customer quotes on the homepage, guarantee and testimonials pages are chosen by Wunderdog.
strengths: A public archive of past Pro Picks going back years, with line, price, units, release time and result on each pick page. Few pick sellers show this much, and the one pick we spot checked was graded correctly.
Advertised long run results are modest, about 52% to 53%, and the about page openly warns that no one hits 60% long term.
Every package is priced on one page, with the dates each season pass covers.
The company replies to negative reviews and has offered free packages to unhappy buyers.
Free picks and a daily email let a reader see the style and the write ups before buying.
concerns: The pick archive is kept and graded by the seller. No outside party confirms it is complete.
The guarantee gives another package, never cash, and the terms say there are no refunds once a product is delivered. Betting losses are never covered.
Even taken at face value, the seller's long run totals show a thin edge, about 2 to 3 cents per unit, that worse prices could erase.
The free picks show a much better record than the paid card, and the Recent Performance box shows a different slice for each sport, so the most visible numbers are the most flattering ones.
Parlay Club wins look high (78%) but come from heavy favorite parlays that need about 75% just to break even.
Marketing numbers change between pages, and the Harvard Business Review case study claim did not match what we could find.
checklist: Open the archive for the sport you want and read the All Picks line, not the free picks, Max Plays or playoff boxes.
Ask for every pick from the last 12 months with the line, the odds and the time it was sent. A list of hot runs is not a record.
Count units, not wins. A 78% parlay record at -300 prices is close to break even.
Read the guarantee for the words refund, credit and extension. Here a losing package earns another package, never money.
Write down each pick yourself the moment you receive it, with the line you can actually get, and compare it with the posted line.
Give any handicapper a few hundred picks before you call them a winner. Short runs swing hard both ways.
faq: It is a real business, Wunderdog Sports Picks LLC, selling picks since 2001 with published prices and a public archive of past picks. We could not independently verify that its picks win over time, because that archive is kept and graded by Wunderdog itself, and its own long run totals sit just above break even.

A handicapper named Geoff, who writes the picks and the analysis. The site gives only his first name; a 2011 betting blog named him as Geoff Kulesa, founder of Wunderdog Sports Picks. The company is Wunderdog Sports Picks LLC, and its terms are governed by Colorado law.

On 20 Nov 2026 single day packages cost $25 to $55, weekly packages $125 to $219, monthly packages $299 to $499, and single sport seasons $499 to $1,399 (prorated as the season goes on). The all sports one year package cost $5,499, and NFL office pool picks cost $15 a week.

No. The terms say there are no refunds once a product is delivered. If a package ends with more units lost than won, you get an equivalent package free, judged in Wunderdog's own units at its posted prices.
Does Wunderdog have a verified record?

Not independently. Wunderdog posts a long pick archive with lines, prices, release times and results, which is more than most sellers show, but no outside party keeps or audits it. On its own figures the NFL card is 3,264-2,905 (52.9%) over 25 years, and no Watchdog graded record is matched to Wunderdog.

For the money you get one handicapper's picks with written analysis, unit sizes and the line at release, plus a free package if a package ends with a unit loss. What is unproven is whether the seller's own small long run edge, about 53% in the NFL, holds up for a buyer who cannot always get the posted price, and the guarantee never returns cash.
